Back to updates Water Column Sonar Data Collection By Data.gov admins · June 09, 2014 NOAA collects and uses active acoustic (or sonar) data for a variety of mapping requirements. As the national archive for multibeam bathymetric data, NGDC manages over 15 million nautical miles of ship trackline data from sources worldwide. In 2011, NGDC, in partnership with NOAA’s National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), initiated a new archive for high resolution data collected with sonars capable of mapping the water column. Water column sonar data are collected on NOAA fishery survey vessels and academic and international fleets, and are used to assess the physical and biological characteristics of the ocean. Primary uses include 3-D mapping of fish schools and other mid-water marine organisms, assessing biological abundance, species identification, and habitat characterization. pages.text: Wayne Rooney: Ex-Manchester United captain considered taking own life during playing career - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Rooney scored 53 goals in 120 appearances for England By Mandeep Sanghera BBC Sport journalist Published 4 hours ago Warning: This article contains references to suicide Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up". The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances. But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast , external , detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby. "When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life. "This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise." The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it". "I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added. "I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well. "I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. pages.text: We depend on plastic. Now we’re drowning in it. | National Geographic By Laura Parker Photographs by Randy Olson Last updated April 8, 2026 This story originally published in the June 2018 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here . If plastic had been invented when the Pilgrims sailed from Plymouth, England, to North America—and the Mayflower had been stocked with bottled water and plastic-wrapped snacks—their plastic trash would likely still be around, four centuries later. If the Pilgrims had been like many people today and simply tossed their empty bottles and wrappers over the side, Atlantic waves and sunlight would have worn all that plastic into tiny bits. And those bits might still be floating around the world’s oceans today, sponging up toxins to add to the ones already in them, waiting to be eaten by some hapless fish or oyster, and ultimately perhaps by one of us. We should give thanks that the Pilgrims didn’t have plastic, I thought recently as I rode a train to Plymouth along England’s south coast. I was on my way to see a man who would help me make sense of the whole mess we’ve made with plastic, especially in the ocean. After sheets of clear plastic trash have been washed in the Buriganga River, in Dhaka, Bangladesh, Noorjahan spreads them out to dry, turning them regularly— while also tending to her son, Momo. The plastic will eventually be sold to a recycler. Less than a fifth of all plastic gets recycled globally. In the U.S. it’s less than 10 percent. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs Wed 18 Nov 2026 06.50 EST Last modified on Wed 18 Nov 2026 07.27 EST Share W hen I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI . But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

It’s called Earth Overshoot Day . In 1971, it fell on Dec. 25. Disturbingly, by 2022, it fell on July 28. In short, we humans need 1.75 Earths to support our current rate of consumption! That is unsustainable, and we have to make changes. So, how can we slow down our current consumption rate, while ensuring equitable progress and resources for all? pages.text: We Sent a Cartographer to the Sale of One of America's Most Famous Maps | National Geographic By Nina Strochlic Published October 29, 2026 1:09 On a spring day in 1982, a never-before-sold piece went under the hammer at Christie's auction house in New York City. In a moment he later said left him breathless, Malcolm Forbes, Jr., the president of Forbes magazine, raised his paddle and won the hand-drawn survey of the Mason-Dixon Line for $360,000—the most ever spent on an American map at the time. The sale shocked bidders: As the price climbed to more than 20 times its estimated sale price, it also managed to overshadow a rare copy of the Declaration of Independence (which fetched $285,000). The losing bidder for the Mason-Dixon map was the Library of Congress. Forbes ended up with an unusual-looking relic: six sheets of paper conjoined into a manuscript just six and a half inches tall and over six feet long. It’s believed to be the only original copy of the western section of the Mason Dixon survey—the most famous border in America. ( Why Your Mental Map of the World Is (Probably) Wrong .) More than 40 years later, that same map has now sold for $1,187,500 to an anonymous buyer, according to Brunk Auctions in North Carolina. The bidding started at $400,000, a sale price that doubled within mere minutes. Today, the Mason-Dixon Line is synonymous with a divided America, and its darkest era. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/wear-and-tear-changes-measurable-pfas-levels-firefighter-hoods-gloves-and NEWS Wear and Tear Changes Measurable PFAS Levels in Firefighter Hoods, Gloves and Wildland Gear May 13, 2026 Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email The protective clothing worn by firefighters often contains a class of chemicals called PFAS. Exposure to PFAS, also known as “forever chemicals,” has been linked to negative health outcomes. In the fourth of an ongoing series of reports, NIST shows that wear and tear increased the levels of PFAS found in hoods and gloves, but it decreased the levels found in wildland gear. A firefighter’s protective clothing is composed of three distinct layers made of different textiles.
